title: Jump Hash & Rendezvous Hashing
description: Compare jump consistent hash, rendezvous hashing, and Maglev hashing against ring-based approaches, with real-world selection criteria.

segments.text: Ring-based consistent hashing is the most famous approach, but it's not the only one. And frankly, for certain workloads, it's not the best one either. Let's look at three alternatives that Google, Akamai, and others chose instead, and understand exactly when each wins.

Jump consistent hash was published by Google in 2014. It's stunningly simple: about five lines of code. Given a key and n buckets, it outputs a bucket number. Uses O of one memory, no ring, no virtual nodes. The algorithm jumps forward through buckets using a pseudorandom sequence until it overshoots n, then returns the last valid bucket.

Jump hash has perfect balance: keys distribute uniformly across buckets with zero variance. And it's fast, O of ln n time. But there's a critical limitation: you can only add or remove the last bucket. If bucket three of ten fails, you can't just remove it. You'd have to rebuild. This makes it ideal for append-only scaling.
segments.thought_prompt: When would append-only bucket management be acceptable? Think about specific infrastructure patterns.

segments.text: Rendezvous hashing, also called highest random weight, takes a different approach. For each key, compute a hash with every server name and pick the server with the highest hash value. It's O of n per lookup, but it gives you arbitrary server removal without the limitations of jump hash.

The O of n lookup cost sounds terrible, but for clusters under a few hundred nodes, it's perfectly fine. Akamai used rendezvous hashing for their CDN because it has zero memory overhead and perfect key distribution. When a server dies, only its keys move, and they distribute uniformly across all remaining servers.

Maglev hashing is Google's solution for their network load balancer. It builds a lookup table where each entry maps to a backend. The table is populated by having each backend fill in entries using a permutation sequence. The result: O of one lookup time with minimal disruption when backends change.

The lookup table size matters. Google uses 65537, a prime number. Bigger tables mean better distribution but more memory and longer build time. When a backend goes down, only one over n entries change, making it nearly as stable as ring-based hashing. Maglev serves all of Google's external traffic, billions of requests per second.

Let's compare head to head. Ring hash: O of log n lookup, O of n memory, arbitrary node removal. Jump hash: O of ln n lookup, O of one memory, append-only. Rendezvous: O of n lookup, O of one memory, arbitrary removal. Maglev: O of one lookup, O of table-size memory, arbitrary removal.
segments.thought_prompt: Given these trade-offs, which would you choose for a 10-node cache cluster? What about a 10,000-node CDN?

segments.text: My selection guide: Use ring hash when you need virtual nodes for heterogeneous servers. Use jump hash for data sharding where nodes only grow, like adding Kafka partitions. Use rendezvous for small clusters needing simplicity. Use Maglev for network load balancers needing O of one lookups at extreme throughput.

Most engineers only learn ring-based consistent hashing. But knowing all four variants makes you dangerous in system design interviews and, more importantly, in production architecture reviews. The right hash strategy can be the difference between a smooth deploy and a thundering herd.
